extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, design patent applicants, patent practitioners, and professional patent draftspersons
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination standards for preparing and examining design patent applications, with rules for drawings, shading, broken lines, surface treatment, photographs/color, statutory subject matter, and computer-generated icons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectional views limited use
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectional views may be included to clarify the shape of the design where the exact contour or configuration of the exterior surface is not apparent from the views of the drawing, but sectional views must not attempt to illustrate features of internal construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Views showing internal construction should be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and cancelled. When a sectional view is added during prosecution, the examiner must determine whether there is antecedent basis in the original disclosure for the material shown in hatching in the sectional view (37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) and MPEP § 608.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading — necessity and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface shading is not required by rule but may be necessary in particular cases to show clearly the character and contour of all surfaces of any 3‑dimensional aspects of the design and to distinguish between open and solid areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use surface shading on unclaimed subject matter shown in broken lines. Lack of appropriate surface shading in the drawing as filed may render the design nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Addition of surface shading after filing may comprise new matter if surface shape is not evident from the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading — prohibited and recommended techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast; oblique line shading must be used to show transparent, translucent, and highly polished or reflective surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast in materials may be shown by using line shading in one area and stippling in another; this technique allows a claim to broadly cover contrasting surfaces without limiting to specific colors or materials, provided the appearance does not patentably depart from the illustrated visual appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 15.49 — Surface Shading Necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing figures should be appropriately and adequately shaded to show clearly the character and/or contour of all surfaces represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular importance for 3D articles to delineate plane, concave, convex, raised and/or depressed surfaces, and to distinguish between open and closed areas. Reiterates prohibition on solid black shading except to represent color black or contrast. (Form paragraph text may be used to notify applicant.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broken lines — permitted purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used to disclose environmental structure related to the claimed design and to define the bounds of the claim; structure not part of the claimed design but necessary to show the environment may be represented in broken lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed subject matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design or of a specified embodiment thereof. A boundary line may be shown in broken lines if it is not intended to form part of the claimed design. Applicant may choose broken-line boundaries where the boundary does not exist in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken-line boundaries — straight vs other shapes and new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no boundary line is shown originally, applicant may amend to add a straight broken line connecting ends of existing full lines defining the claimed subject matter; any broken line boundary other than a straight broken line may constitute new matter prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious adding broken-line boundaries other than straight lines; examiners should consider potential new matter objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines must not indicate unimportance or show hidden planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines are not permitted for the purpose of indicating that a portion of an article is of less importance in the design, nor may they be used to show hidden planes and surfaces that cannot be seen through opaque materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of broken lines indicates that the depicted structure forms no part of the design and is not to indicate relative importance of parts. See In re Blum and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines — crossing full lines and disclosure clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When broken lines cross over the full-line showing of the claimed design, the purpose of those broken lines must be explicitly identified in the specification so that the scope of the claim is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If broken lines crossing over the design are defined as environment, the surface beneath is part of the claimed design; if defined as boundaries, the area within broken lines is not part of the claimed design. If broken lines obscure clear understanding, include separate figure(s) showing the claimed design without the broken lines. Do not use surface shading on unclaimed subject matter shown in broken lines to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 15.50 — Design Claimed Shown in Full Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornamental design which is being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing; dotted lines for indicating unimportant or immaterial features are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no portions of a claimed design which are immaterial or unimportant. Use this paragraph to notify applicant when claim lines are not shown properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 15.50.02 — Description of Broken Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The following statement must be used to describe the broken lines on the drawing: '-- The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design. --' (Insert name of structure and whether showing portions of the article or environment.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement must be inserted in the specification preceding the claim to clarify the role of broken lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectionable use of broken lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Dotted lines or broken lines used for environmental structure should not cross or intrude upon the representation of the claimed design, since they may obscure the claimed design and render the disclosure indefinite (35 U.S.C. 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such intrusion occurs, require separate figures or appropriate amendments to clarify the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment — definition and statutory limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface treatment (shape/configuration as well as indicia, contrasting color or materials, graphic representations, or other ornamentation applied to the article) must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment alone (not applied to an article) is not proper design patent subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface treatment must be shown in full lines or in broken lines (if unclaimed) to meet statutory requirement. Guidelines for computer-generated icons apply equally to surface treatment disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment — evidentiary effect and amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of surface treatment in a design drawing or photograph will normally be considered prima facie evidence that the inventor considered the surface treatment integral to the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments canceling two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines will be permitted if it is clear applicant had possession of the underlying configuration without the surface treatment. Removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to the configuration (e.g., beading, grooves, ribs) will introduce prohibited new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and color drawings — when acceptable and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are normally required in black ink on white paper; photographs are acceptable only when the invention is not capable of being illustrated in an ink drawing or where the invention is shown more clearly in a photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b). Color photographs/color drawings require a petition under 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2) with fee, three sets of color drawings/photos, and a specification statement that the file contains at least one color drawing/photograph. Poor photographic quality that fails to reproduce details can lead to objections and rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs). Photographs and ink drawings must not be combined in one application formal submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color lining, informal color drawings, and later omission of color
rubrics_metrics.description: Color may be shown in pen and ink drawings by lining surfaces according to symbols; if formal drawings are lined for color, insert 'The drawing is lined for color.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lining entire surfaces for color may interfere with clear showing of design because surface shading cannot be used simultaneously to define contours. A surface may be partially lined with a statement that color extends across entire surface, or a separate view omitting color but properly shaded may be submitted for clarity. If color drawings/photos are filed originally, color is integral; omission of color later is permitted only if underlying configuration without color is clearly shown in the original disclosure. Informal color photographs/drawings may be accepted for filing-date purposes but require steps to convert to formal drawings later (petition, fee, statement, three full sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination prerequisites — statutory requirements for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent applications ornamentality, novelty, nonobviousness, enablement and definiteness are necessary prerequisites to grant of a patent; inventive novelty/unobviousness resides in ornamental shape/configuration or surface ornamentation applied to an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/nonobviousness determinations generally require searches in pertinent design classes and mechanical classes, and consultation of catalogs, trade journals and available foreign patent databases. If statutory requirements are not met, examiner must set forth basis for rejections in detail in Office action. If claim is patentable but formal matters remain, issue Ex parte Quayle actions (allowability subject to formal corrections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action and prosecution practice (Quayle, summary statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim does not satisfy statutory requirements the examiner will set forth the basis for all rejections. If claim is patentable but formal matters remain, send Ex parte Quayle action indicating allowability and necessary corrections. Use specified form paragraphs for summary statements of rejections and allowability indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reply to an Office action overcomes a rejection, indicate that the rejection is withdrawn in the next Office action unless a notice of allowability. If a later rejection is required after a Quayle indication, withdraw allowability and reopen prosecution with appropriate form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro se applicant guidance — employing counsel and draftspersons
rubrics_metrics.description: In pro se design applications examiners should notify applicant that it may be desirable to employ a registered patent attorney/agent or professional patent draftsperson to prepare formal drawings, and include the 'Guide To Filing A Design Patent Application' where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs 15.66 and 15.66.01 may be used in the first Office action when patentable subject matter appears present and disclosure complies with 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171 — types of designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The language 'new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture' includes at least: (A) a design for an ornament, impression, print, or picture applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture (surface indicia); (B) a design for the shape or configuration of an article of manufacture; and (C) a combination of the first two categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A picture standing alone is not patentable; the distinguishing factor is embodiment of the design in an article of manufacture. Claims to picture/print per se should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 as nonstatutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated icons — article of manufacture requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications for computer-generated icons must comply with the 'article of manufacture' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 171; icons alone are surface ornamentation and not statutory, but icons embodied in a computer screen, monitor, other display panel, or a portion thereof may be statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer-generated icon must be embodied in a computer screen/monitor/display panel (or portion) to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 171. The dependence of such icons on hardware/software for existence is not a bar to being a design for an article of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for examining computer-generated icon applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the entire disclosure to determine what is claimed and whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture; review drawings for depiction of a computer screen/monitor/display panel or portion; ensure sufficient number of views and compliance with 37 CFR 1.84; review title and specification for characteristic feature statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles like 'computer icon' are inadequate; titles must indicate embodiment (e.g., 'computer screen with an icon'). If drawing does not depict embodiment, reject under 35 U.S.C. 171; if disclosure suggests embodiment, suggest amendments. Indicate all formal objections under 37 CFR rules and upon applicant reply enter amendments and reassess entire record. Withdraw rejection if applicant establishes embodiment by a preponderance of evidence (In re Oetiker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of type fonts and changeable icons
rubrics_metrics.description: Type fonts historically have been granted design patents and should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 solely because modern typesetting is computer-generated. Computer-generated icons that change in appearance during viewing may be claimed by showing sequential views; the transitional process/period is not part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification describing the transitional nature and that the process/period of transition forms no part of the claimed design; examples of acceptable descriptive statements are provided in the guidelines.
